Most films about the Nazi regime are either brilliant or total crap. All dramas about the Nazi regime are crap. This is because the genre conventions of drama always imply that the Holocaust, in and of itself, wasn’t sad enough and needed to be "spiced up" with dramatic elements. This isn’t a moralistic stance on my part; it’s simply a semiotic observation. Here is a list of brilliant and shitty films about the Nazi regime: Shitty: *The Pianist*, *Schindler’s List*, *Downfall*, *The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas*. Brilliant: *Shoah*, *Night and Fog*, *Inglourious Basterds*, *The Zone of Interest*, *Salò*, *The Night Porter*, *The White Ribbon*, *Images of the World and the Inscription of War*, *Histoire(s) du cinéma*. What do the brilliant films have in common? They are abstractions and never attempt to derive an emotional "punchline" from war crimes.

The Germans, meanwhile, are comically evil as always, and taking away their humanity actually just makes it seem dramatic and fake. Not to mention the Roman Polanski of it all. I’ll take Woody any day over this crap. If they’re both pedos, at least the latter never tried a Holocaust movie. Any attempt at Holocaust cinema became inutile after the benchmark of Night and Fog, in which Alain Resnais proved the exclusivity of banality and silence for the sub-genre. Yet, Roman Polanski and Steven Spielberg, two great Jewish Hollywood auteurs, instantly turned into foolish Anglophone monsters at the sight of award-season potential—with one borrowing sight, and the other form, from a common evil denominator: the Eastern European New Wave. If Polanski comes out as the lesser devil in this scandal-off, that's owing to his own Eastern European background, which allows him to see through the insincerity of his predecessors. Still, when a highly audience-friendly biopic relies this much on shock value and historical reenactment, Jacques Rivette's critique of the Holocaust cinema of his own era still rings true, and Resnais's long-lasting legacy continues to resonate. If anything, this, along with J'accuse, serves as an integral part of Polanski's auteurism, where a traceable fear of the "arbitrary" haunts him, both as a Jew and as a criminal. Naturally, a sense of victimhood permeates his cinema, where a cosmic connection with accused Jewish figures in history enables him to navigate through a personal war—one for which he turns out to be the villain after all.

Despite the gravity of its subject matter, The Pianist unfortunately feels artificial in its execution. The dialogue is often stiff and awkwardly theatrical while several supporting characters verge on caricature. The result is a dramatisation that favours recognisable conventions over psychological complexity. Even Adrien Brody’s performance, for which he won numerous awards is neither exceptional nor particularly multifaceted. The film follows a linear progression of persecution, escape and survival, with successive episodes arranged as increasingly harrowing dramatic set pieces - all effective when it comes to building tension yet leaving the viewer with a feeling that the whole thing is overly formulaic. Most problematically, the film’s stylised depiction of suffering and hardships turns the historical misery into spectacle. It comes perilously close to misery porn. Symbolism is so clearly signposted that it feels imposed rather than discovered and minor gestures are inflated into moments of enormous significance. It‘s annoying! Another particularly frustrating aspect is the film’s inconsistent and occasionally illogical use of language and dialect/accent (the question of which character speaks which language is handled in a way that often feels arbitrary). „The Pianist“ frequently resembles a conventional television production (including awful visual effects) rather than a truly accomplished work of cinema. Its visual style is neither competent nor rarely distinctive, while its dialogue, characterisation and narrative structure rely almost painfully on familiar dramatic conventions. All these aspects undermine the credibility of the world the film seeks to establish. More broadly, it leaves few clichés unexploited. Disappointing and highly irritating!

Revi O Pianista por conta do Thomas Kretschmann, já que a primeira e única vez que eu tinha assistido foi aos 13 anos e nem fazia ideia de quem era ele na época. E continuo achando um dos filmes sobre o Holocausto que eu menos gosto, perdendo apenas para O Menino do Pijama Listrado. Para mim, a obra do Roman Polanski é um retrato presunçoso da crueldade, caindo diretamente no que muitos críticos chamam de "pornografia da dor". A câmera se demora na miséria e no sadismo de forma quase voyeurística, chocando pelo grotesco em vez de focar na profundidade psicológica ou na resistência real das vítimas. O protagonista, Władysław Szpilman, passa o filme inteiro sendo um observador passivo da própria tragédia. Ele não age, não luta e não tem nem compaixão apenas é jogado de um esconderijo para outro e sobrevive por puro acaso e sorte. Isso deixa a narrativa fria, incômoda e vazia de calor humano. Me choca até hoje o Adrien Brody ter levado o Oscar por interpretar o que parece ser apenas uma casca oca em tela kkk. Quando a gente compara esse estilo com um filme recente como A Zona de Interesse, fica escancarado o quanto o cinema pode abordar a Segunda Guerra de forma muito mais inteligente. Enquanto Polanski apela para o espetáculo visual da dor e o choque escancarado, A Zona de Interesse pega essa exata ideia da frieza e da banalidade do mal e faz algo infinitamente superior e mais assustador. O horror do Holocausto não precisa ser esfregado na sua cara, ele está no som de fundo, na rotina alienada da família e na indiferença assustadora com o vizinho do lado. Gostei apenas da cena que ele volta a tocar o piano depois de anos, aquilo ali sim foi bonito de ser ver. Gostaria que tivessem focado mais nessa ausência da música na vida dele e como isso afetou ele psicologicamente, mas nem tudo são flores. O Pianista prefere se apoiar na exploração estética da crueldade do que na construção de um drama humano denso. Talvez um dia eu tenha outra visão dessa alegoria holocaustica de um diretor pedófilo, mas por hora é isso. A experiência de rever só reafirmou que o choque gratuito nunca vai substituir o verdadeiro terror psicológico.

This just isn’t that good, and that’s not even mentioning its director. I got an awkward feeling when watching this, a second hand embarrassment of sorts that feels like it’s using this horrific episode of history as a means to generate a reaction from the audience, rather than sincerely. Regardless of the many historical inaccuracies, which admittedly even better films are often punctuated with, it’s a film that someone seems outdated today when by all means it should feel more relevant than ever. It’s narrative, while being one of loss, also feels fairly episodic, and without time for deeper reflection on its subject matter. One may argue, and I can certainly see how, that this film is meant to put the audience in the shoes of it’s protagonist, and there are effective ways in which it does this - for example by leaving German speech in German while using English to portray Polish - however I found the idea impossible to believe because the characters consistently talk as if they are from 2000s. This criticism is less about the structure of the language, and rather its substance - characters speak as if they have read history textbooks on Nazi Germany and WW2, and they speak about racism and bigotry with a 2000s understanding, and as if it were invented by the Nazis uniquely, rather than the reality of being something Jewish people have faced for a millennia. The episodic nature of the narrative does not help this “textbook” feel, as if it were designed to be shown in schools as a timeline of Warsaw under German occupation, with such large time jumps in which seemingly nothing changes in the characters or the world they inhabit. None of this is helped by the film’s visuals, which come across as generic and flat. I’m reminded of Schindler’s List, a film I would consider superior because of its better awareness of how to treat its subject matter - the visuals are appropriate, the character study of Oscar Schindler is done better and more engaging, and characters feel far more real and of their time than here. A biting example is the Schindler’s List’s colour palate, using the red of a girl’s coat to deliver an emotional impact far more effective than any in this film. This film firmly sits with The Rise of Evil in a category of WW2 films that don’t do their depictions of it justice in an awkwardly embarrassing way.

The true story of Wladyslaw Szpilman is used more broadly to make a solid drama which realistically portrays a very important time and place in World War II and the Holocaust which is otherwise given short shrift by American and Western European filmmakers. (I consider myself a fairly well-read layperson but did not know, for example, that following the Warsaw ghetto uprising and the broader Warsaw uprising - which I didn't even realise were separate events - the Germans razed the entire city in response.) It ranks alongside Schindler's List and Zone of Interest as Holocaust films which are highly technically competent, and capital-I Important, but do not actually do much as stories beyond presenting the horror of what occurred. Now, secondarily - and spoilers ensue - in the closing half hour the starving and half-dead Szpilman finds himself, hunting for food in the deserted and bombed-out ruins of Warsaw, face-to-face with a German officer. The officer listens to him play the piano, is moved to tears, and ultimately helps Szpilman remain concealed and even brings him food. While watching this - and specifically the implication that Szpilman's artistry reminded the Nazi of a Jew's fundamental humanity - I frowned, and was reminded of one of the closing chapters of Herman Wouk's novel War and Remembrance, in which a Nazi officer recognises the Jewish writer Aaron Jastrow while they are en route to Auschwitz, invites him into the officer's car, has a civilised conversation with him about literature and art and politics... yet still ushers him off to a certain death, not with hatred but with indifference. This was in real life a more common attitude among Nazis, I imagine, and I was ready to write off The Pianist's meeting in the ruins as the poetic license of a soppy Hollywood script. But here's the thing, this being one of those movies that sends you off to Wikipedia once the credits roll: it actually happened. The officer's name was Wilm Hosenfeld, Szpilman wasn't the only Jew he assisted, and he was named as one of the Righteous Among the Nations. It all actually happened, right down to the specific Chopin piece Szpilman played for him. And here's another thing: Polanski himself is a Holocaust survivor. His mother went to the gas chambers and he lived through these same years in Poland as a miserable child in hiding from the Nazis. And yet. The film lingers so much on Hosenfeld in its closing moments - the mercy and kindness he displays, the family photo on his desk, Szpilman's visit to the field where his POW camp was - that I began to get a notion of what drew Polanski to this *particular* Polish Holocaust story, one which takes outsized importance in the movie's dragnet. It should not be surprising that a fugitive who raped a 13-year-old girl while he himself was 43 should be interested in stories about forgiveness. But Hosenfeld faced justice, albeit a rough and brutal Soviet justice. Polanski, on the other hand, fled the jurisdiction and has evaded justice ever since. The Pianist is a good film, and perhaps the Hosenfeld angle is coincidental, but it continues to baffle me that Polanski had any career at all after 1977 - that seemingly decent men like Adrien Brody went on to set every day in 2002 to begin just another working day with a man who raped a child - and it left a sour taste in my mouth that in even a subconscious way Polanski might have laid his hands upon a real story about two real people meeting in the ruins of Warsaw, in the closing days of the most terrible and important thing that has ever happened, because he drew some metaphorical association with his own plight. A good movie by a bad person.

The Pianist is at its best when it stops documenting the Holocaust and starts exploring what it means to survive it. I found the first half surprisingly tedious, not because it spends too much time on the persecution itself, but because it spends so much time ticking off each stage of its escalation without sufficiently exploring its human impact. The restrictions, the Star of David, the ghetto, the deportations: each stage is presented almost as another item on a checklist, another example of how discrimination escalated, another opportunity to shock the audience. Having visited Auschwitz and Dachau, studied the Holocaust extensively, and seen Schindler’s List more than once, I didn’t need another chronological illustration of its horrors. I wanted to understand what these experiences did to the people living through them. Too often, the film seems more interested in showing us the next atrocity than in developing a deeper understanding of its characters. That’s where Spielberg succeeds where Polanski, for me, falls short. Schindler’s List gives its historical events a powerful emotional and dramatic core, whereas The Pianist too often feels like it’s ticking off historical checkpoints. The issue isn’t that Polanski shows too much of the persecution, but that he rarely gives its individual stages enough emotional depth to justify the attention they receive. I kept wondering whether the film could have achieved more by spending less time illustrating the different forms of oppression and more time exploring how they gradually dismantled the lives, relationships and identities of the people experiencing them. The second half, however, won me over to a considerable extent. Once Szpilman is forced into hiding, the film becomes much more engaging, and I particularly liked the later sequences that experiment with silence, restricted perspective and the tension of Szpilman navigating a hostile, deserted city. Still, even here, I wanted more of the mundane reality of hiding: the hours of boredom, the routines, the psychological toll of doing absolutely nothing while knowing that a single mistake could get you killed. Instead, Polanski often jumps between the major turning points, leaving me wishing he had spent more time simply observing the everyday experience of survival. That, to me, is precisely where a fictional film can offer something a documentary cannot: not just an account of what happened, but an intimate character study of what it meant to live through it. Adrien Brody delivers an excellent performance, and the production design, costumes and sets are consistently convincing. There is plenty to admire here, and the film becomes considerably more engaging as it narrows its focus to Szpilman’s immediate struggle to survive. Nevertheless, I found The Pianist less successful than Schindler’s List at transforming historical horror into a compelling cinematic experience. A good film about an important subject is not necessarily a great film simply because of the subject it tackles.

C'est un film avec un interet historique important, notamment car il représente un témoignage direct des actes de violences orchestrés par les nazis dans les ghettos, précisément dans celui de Varsovie, avec une violence énorme, des grandes famines et les ravages causés par les maladies. Des images qui restent difficiles à voir, avec des scènes dramatiques de violences, d'humiliations subies par le peuple juif qui sont d'une exceptionnelle cruauté. Je recommande, d'une part car meme sans tenir compte de la réalité historique du film, l'histoire demeure intéressante et profonde, avec une mise en contexte et un cadre de chaos national en Pologne qui est très bien réalisée. D'autre part, je recommande car le film est donc basé sur un témoignage officiel, élément important et fiable pour comprendre l'ampleur de la violence exceptionnelle des nazis, de plus, le film montre je trouve assez bien le statut de "sous homme" ou "race inférieure" administé aux Juifs pendant la 2nd Guerre Mondiale. Un film qui est long, environ 2h30, mais il vaut le coup si vous avez le temps.

Honestly, I don’t even know how to properly rate this film. The Pianist is one of those movies where, at certain points, I genuinely considered stopping because of how difficult it was to watch. Not because it was bad, but because what was being portrayed was just so incredibly painful. We know the story. We know the historical events, and we’ve seen countless other films about the Holocaust. And yet, The Pianist managed to affect me in a way that felt incredibly raw and personal. The images of Warsaw in ruins, people lying dead in the streets, the gradual dehumanization, and the way people were stripped of their dignity, their identity, and ultimately their humanity. It was absolutely devastating to watch. Adrien Brody’s performance was phenomenal. The way he portrayed the physical and psychological deterioration of Władysław Szpilman was particularly powerful. Watching a once-independent, talented man slowly become someone whose entire existence revolves around simply staying alive was heartbreaking. I find it incredibly difficult to evaluate a film like this using conventional movie criteria. Of course, you can talk about the cinematography, the performances, the direction, and the storytelling. But ultimately, what stays with me is the feeling of having witnessed something I almost couldn’t bear to watch, yet felt I needed to see. And that’s exactly why I’m giving it five stars. Not because I enjoyed watching it. Not because anything about it was beautiful or entertaining. But because it managed to convey something so horrific, so deeply disturbing, and so profoundly human that I couldn’t simply look away. And finally: Fuck Roman Polanski.

So oft finde ich, dass sich Filme „einfach so weggucken“. Wenn ich für dieses Phänomen ein Gegenbeispiel nennen müsste, wäre das wohl „Der Pianist“. Hier löst jede Szene etwas in der Zuschauerschaft aus, dennoch fällt es mir schwer über diesen Film zu sprechen. Mir fällt es deswegen schwer, da es so gut wie unmöglich ist, den Film außerhalb des historischen Kontextes - und damit „nur“ als Film - wahrzunehmen. Das ist natürlich auch nicht die Intention des Films, doch will ich den Film als solchen bewerten. Das hängt hauptsächlich damit zusammen, dass die Geschichte dermaßen einnehmend ist, dass alle anderen Aspekte (außer das Schauspiel) in den Hintergrund rücken. Teilweise sind Handlungen dermaßen abscheulich, dass es sich fast nach einem satirischen Kommentar anfühlt - einer Utopie wie man sie aus den „Hunger Games“ kennt - schrecklicher Weise beruht das Ganze auf wahren Begebenheiten. Das verschlägt einem immer wieder die Sprache. Nun klingt es doch absurd einen solchen Film nach kinematographischen Maßstäben zu bewerten, weshalb ich mir eher die Frage stellte, was man hätte anders erzählen können. So fehlt mir ein wenig der emotionale Bezug zu den einzelnen Charakteren, nicht dass der Film nicht auch ohne diesen mitreißend und tragisch ist, doch wäre es so noch intensiver, den Leidensweg der Nebenfiguren zu begleiten. Vielleicht aber ist es auch genau diese Banalität dahinter, dass es egal ist was einen Menschen ausmacht, dieser ausschließlich auf sein „Jude-sein“ reduziert wird und das Grund genug ist, ihn leiden und sterben zu lassen. Aus dieser Überlegung wurde ich also auch nicht schlau, noch immer konnte ich nicht „rational“ beschreiben, wie ich diesen Film finde. Das bringt mich zurück zum Anfangsgedanken. Denn eigentlich macht auch genau das Filme im Wesen aus - es ist das, was ein Film im Publikum selbst auslöst. „Der Pianist“ ist packend, herzzerreißend, erschreckend echt und eine absolute Pflicht in der historischen Aufklärung über das NS-Regime.
